title: Never compete on price alone: how low prices work as the outcome of a strategy
summary: Jason Cohen explains why "never compete on price" is right for commoditized markets but wrong when low price is the outcome of interlocking trade-offs, as at Costco, Southwest, Vanguard and IKEA. He covers the price-cut math, why weaknesses deter copycats, and seven shared traits that let bootstrappers pull this off.

principles.text: Price cuts hurt more than they look: a 20% cut needs 25% more customers just to hold revenue.
principles.quote: A 20% price cut needs a 25% increase in number-of-customers to maintain the same amount revenue.

principles.text: Even a small price cut can gut profit, since it comes straight out of margin.
principles.quote: even a seemingly-minor 10% price reduction can easily mean a 50% profit reduction

principles.text: Low price works only as one outcome of a comprehensive strategy, not as a last-ditch tactic against competitors.
principles.quote: successful low-price strategies treat price as just one component of a comprehensive strategy to win.

principles.text: Build strategy on deliberate trade-offs. Weaknesses that some customers hate are what stop copycats.
principles.quote: Others want to copy strengths, but won't copy weaknesses. Because the weaknesses were mandatory to produce their strengths, they were never replicated.

principles.text: Bootstrappers underprice from fear and ignorance, attracting the worst customers and leaving no money to reinvest.
principles.quote: Low prices leave room for neither reinvestment nor profit.

principles.text: A sustainable low-price model needs healthy unit economics from early on, not only at scale. Reinvest profits and expand gradually.
principles.quote: Profitable unit economics, with GPM above 70%, with a CAC payback period of less than a year.
